Hi [CLIENT_NAME_003], Thank you for getting in touch. I’d be glad to assist with this.

For financial model reviews, my usual rate is $10/hour. I work hourly rather than charging a flat fee because a financial model cannot really be reviewed by simply "spot checking" one part. One incorrect input or formula can flow through the entire model, so reviewing it properly requires checking it from beginning to end and correcting or strengthening anything necessary along the way.

For your particular model, I would compare the entered data against the source documents, verify that formulas and links operate correctly between sheets, and review the main assumptions for reasonableness and adequate support. I would also thoroughly assess the valuation components—including WACC, cost of equity, Beta, and their application—as well as the tax treatment, since minor mistakes in these areas can remain hidden until they distort the outputs.

After you provide the template and data, I can briefly examine them and estimate the likely number of hours, giving you a clearer cost expectation before work begins.

Please let me know whether this arrangement suits you, and send the files whenever you are ready.

Best,
[FREELANCER_NAME_002]

After examining the other 2 files, I determined that the excel template you provided is a standard single-highway toll-road PPP model, specifically a generic PPIAF/Operis educational template. It was not designed for your fleetpods setup involving 8 sites, several revenue sources (parking, pods, fleet subscriptions, digital platform, EV charging), and an availability-payment framework comparing Case A with Case B. Therefore, this is more than a task of correcting a few errors. The model requires a substantial rebuild using the template's financial engine—its debt schedule and 3-statement structure—while replacing the payment, capex, and revenue modules to align with your requirements.

Based on my current understanding, the scope would include, but not be limited to:
\- Building capex/opex by site for the gateway, regional, and corridor-support typologies
\- Modeling every revenue stream: parking, pods, fleet contracts, digital, and ancillary
\- Developing the capital stack and debt schedule, with DSCR/IRR outputs
\- Sizing the availability payment endogenously to a target DSCR of 1.3-1.4x
\- Comparing Case A (user-funded) against Case B (PPP with availability payment)
\- Running sensitivities for traffic, occupancy, capex, interest rate, and opex
\- Producing clean, presentation-ready formatting suitable for submission to government

Before beginning, I will require the following from you:
\- The referenced feasibility/demand study, Fleetpod-Demand-Analysis
\- Agreed point estimates for the principal inputs, because the brief currently provides ranges. I will need either confirmed base-case values or approval to use the midpoints I choose

Timeline: approximately 30-45 hours, or about 5-7 days, depending on the speed at which the inputs are confirmed.

Rate: $10/hour, invoiced through milestones covering the structure build, revenue/payment logic, Case A/B & sensitivities, final formatting, and Dashboards. This will allow you to monitor both progress and cost throughout the work.

If helpful, I am available for a brief call before starting to verify the scope.

Best,
[FREELANCER_NAME_002]

4) No financing terms have been finalized, and there are currently no lender or investor commitments. Please use standard market assumptions drawn from the supplied ranges.

5) Structured site-level information, including traffic counts and land status, is not currently available. We only have a general traffic count by corridor; because site-level details are unavailable, they will need to be modelled.

7) The model must clearly establish and justify why availability-style payments are required to make the project viable and bankable. THIS IS THE CORE INFORMATION THE GOVERNMENT WANTS TO SEE, so it needs to be modelled correctly.

Please clarify the following items:
1. Conflicting site lists
The Demand Analysis report and Business Case present two distinct 8-site networks. The Demand Analysis contains Bowden-Lacombe, Wetaskiwin-Ponoka, Bassano, and Atmore, while the Business Case instead includes Red Deer, Fort McMurray-Suncor, and Medicine Hat. For the financial model, should the Business Case list be considered final because it includes the capital allocation amounts?

2. Conflicting opex amounts
The initial brief gives steady-state operating costs of CAD 30-40M/year across the 8-site network. However, Appendix 1 of the Business Case reports annual O&M of just CAD 2.8-3.9M/year, which is an approximately 9x variance. Which amount, or underlying cost basis, should be applied as the financial model's operating cost assumption?

3. Target for availability payment sizing
Do you want the availability payment calculated solely to meet the current minimum DSCR target of 1.35x, or should it also target a minimum equity IRR? The Business Case specifies an infrastructure-equity target range of 12-18%. With the present DSCR-only method, the equity IRR remains negative even when the availability payment is included.

4. Shared/programwide costs
Within the $155M Reference Case, the Business Case includes $11.6M of shared programwide expenses for the digital platform and program management, as well as a $9M reserve/9th-site allowance, in addition to $134.5M of site-level capex. Should these be shown as distinct model line items, or do they fall outside the scope of the 8-site financial model?

5. Confirmation of financing assumptions
According to the Business Case, senior debt represents 60-75% of capital and is priced at 200-300bps above Government of Canada bond yields, with mezzanine debt as an option. Our current simplified assumption is a 70/30 debt/equity structure using a flat 6%. At this stage, should mezzanine be shown as its own layer, or can we retain the simplified single-tranche approach?

6. Depreciation and tax
At present, we use a flat 25% tax on EBITDA and have not yet included a depreciation shield. Is this sufficient for this phase, or, because the model is intended for an actual government submission, should depreciation/CCA (Capital Cost Allowance) be incorporated?

1\. Site list
The model should follow the Business Case site list.

2\. Opex figures
For the correct program-level operating assumption, apply the CAD 30–40M/year range in the original brief. The Appendix amount appears incomplete or understated and must not be used for the complete network model.

3\. Availability payment approach
Calculate the availability payment so that it meets both of these thresholds:

\- A minimum DSCR of approximately 1.35x, and

\-bA minimum equity IRR within the 12–15% range. Do not base the model only on DSCR when that produces negative equity returns.

4\. Program-wide/shared costs
Show the digital platform, program management, and contingency/reserve as separate model line items. They form part of total program capex and should not be left out.

5\. Financing structure
For now, the simplified 70/30 debt/equity structure at approximately 6% is fine. Mezzanine does not need to be modeled as a separate layer yet; keep the structure streamlined until lenders are engaged, at which point we can refine it.

6\. Tax/depreciation
Incorporate CCA/depreciation correctly by applying the standard Canadian Capital Cost Allowance classes relevant to each asset type, such as Class 1 for buildings, Class 43 for clean energy equipment, and Class 8 for furniture/fixtures, among any others that apply. This is critical to a credible government submission and will have a material impact on both the tax shield and equity returns.

The immediate objective is to produce a coherent base-case model promptly and then refine it through iteration.

While completing the model, remember that the figures remain projections. At this point, our main objective is to give the government sufficiently robust financial information to clearly support the need for an availability-style payment. The model must plainly show that user fees by themselves cannot make the project viable and bankable.

Hi [CLIENT_NAME_002],

Of course, I will implement the requested revisions. The reason the model appears detailed is that it uses separate drivers: every revenue category (parking, pods, fleet, digital, ancillary) and every cost line is individually calculated from its corresponding assumption instead of being entered as a single lump-sum figure. This was intentional, because if a government reviewer asks, "where does this figure come from?", each amount can be traced to its source in the Assumptions tab. That traceability is what makes the model defensible.

The drawback is the one you have identified: using more drivers creates more rows to review. I am comfortable taking either approach, so I would like you to choose between:

(a) Retaining the driver-based structure, which is more defensible but contains more rows, or
(b) Converting it into a summary model with only a few high-level lines—total revenue, total cost, debt, availability payment, and returns—while placing the detailed calculations in hidden/backing tabs. This would make the front page concise and clean without removing the underlying detail for anyone who wishes to inspect it.

I can therefore create a one-pager while preserving the supporting audit trail. Let me know your preference, and I will reorganize the model on that basis.

Several structural possibilities also arose that may materially strengthen the government proposal. They have not yet been included in the model; I am raising them because any one of them could help distinguish the submission. For example:

1\. Government-funds-first, followed by subletting against income ("build-then-transfer"). The Province provides or co-provides the upfront capex, using the cheapest available capital, and subsequently leases/sublets the operating network to a private operator. The operator then pays a concession fee from parking, pod, and fleet revenues. This reverses the narrative: rather than the government paying out an availability payment, it receives a return. I could add this as a third scenario, Case C, which may indicate a substantially lower net cost to the Province than the availability-payment structure.

2\. An availability payment initially, followed by a later transition to revenue sharing. Instead of keeping the payment flat for 30-year, the Province could contribute more during the early ramp-up period when revenue is limited. Once the network reaches maturity and produces excess cash, the Province would participate in the upside and recover a portion of its prior payments. This preserves bankability, lowers the lifetime net cost, and presents the arrangement as a partnership instead of a subsidy.

3\. A toll / user-levy applied to the corridor. Where the sites are situated on designated freight corridors, a small levy per truck—or part of an existing road-use fee—could be ring-fenced to partially finance the network. This would directly lower the availability payment funded from general government revenue by requiring benefiting users to contribute.

4\. A phased equity sale / refinancing upon stabilisation. The model could assume that, once construction is complete and risk has declined around year 5-7, the Province or initial equity holders sell part of their interest to a pension fund or infrastructure fund. Stabilized infrastructure producing cash yields can be sold at a premium, allowing the original capital to be withdrawn at a profit and reinvested in Phase 2 rather than remaining committed for 30 years.

5\. Revenue from anchor / cornerstone tenants. Before financial close, one or two major fleets or a fuel/EV/retail partner could enter a long-term take-or-pay agreement for the main hubs. A relatively modest guaranteed revenue floor can materially improve DSCR and reduce the availability payment required by lenders. It is the quickest method of strengthening the figures without altering the build.

I would be happy to include any of these as extra model cases. Options 1 and 2, in particular, may significantly reduce the stated cost to government, which could make the submission more persuasive. Please advise which direction you want to pursue and whether you prefer the simplified structure (b) or the detailed version, and I will revise it accordingly.

Best,

I sent that second deliverable before you asked for this refund. Despite my requests, I received no specific review comments on either the first draft or the second version.

Because both milestones were completed and delivered according to scope, I will not issue a refund. I will take this through Upwork's dispute process to settle the outstanding milestone payment.
